source_refs.note: Topic 5.12 with Figs. 5.17 to 5.23 and the Interesting Information box (PDF 109-112, printed 106-109). The Torricelli text cites 'Fig. 6.4', which does not exist in this chapter; recorded as a finding.

blocks.text: A number of devices operate by means of the pressure difference that results from changes in the speed of the fluid.

items: Aeroplane wings (Fig. 5.17): the wing is designed to deflect the air so that the streamlines are closer together above the wing than below it. Where the streamlines are forced closer together the speed is faster, so air travels faster on the upper side of the wing than on the lower; the pressure is lower at the top of the wing, the wing is forced upward, and the lift of an aeroplane is due to this effect. (Why are wings rounded outward and flattened inward? The curved upper surface lengthens the path and crowds the streamlines above the wing.)

Swing of a ball (Fig. 5.18): when a ball is thrown or kicked with spin, the ball is made smoother on one side by the bowler and remains rough on the other. The air moves faster over the rough side and slows over the smoother; by Bernoulli's equation the faster-moving air creates lower pressure while the slower air creates higher pressure, and this pressure difference generates a sideways force, the Magnus effect, which causes the ball to curve in the air.

Filter pump (Fig. 5.19): a filter pump has a constriction in the centre, so that a jet of water from the tap flows faster there. This causes a drop in pressure near it and air therefore flows in from the side tube; the air and water together are expelled through the lower part of the pump.

Carburetor (Fig. 5.20): the carburetor of a car engine uses a Venturi duct to feed the correct mixture of air and petrol to the cylinders. Air is drawn through the duct and along a pipe to the cylinders, and a tiny inlet at the side of the duct is fed with petrol. The air through the duct moves very fast, creating low pressure in the duct, which draws petrol vapours into the air stream.

Paint sprayer (Fig. 5.21): a stream of air passing over a tube dipped in a liquid causes the liquid to rise in the tube. This effect is used in perfume bottles and paint sprayers: when the rubber ball of an atomizer is squeezed the air is blown through the tube and rushes out through the narrow aperture at high speed, causing a fall of pressure, so the atmospheric pressure pushes the perfume up leading to the narrow aperture.
Venturi relation (Fig. 5.22): a horizontal pipe with a wide section A1 and a narrow section A2, whose pressures a manometer compares; derived below.
Torricelli's theorem (Fig. 5.23): the speed of efflux from a small orifice in a tank; derived below.

blocks.text: Consider a pipe in which a fluid of density rho flows through different areas of cross-section (Fig. 5.22): A1 at the wide end and A2 at the narrow portion, with flow speeds v1 and v2 and pressures P1 and P2 indicated by the limbs of a manometer. As the pipe is horizontal, the average potential energy is the same at both places, so Bernoulli's equation gives P1 + (1/2) rho v1^2 = P2 + (1/2) rho v2^2, or P1 - P2 = (1/2) rho v2^2 - (1/2) rho v1^2, or P1 - P2 = (1/2) rho (v2^2 - v1^2) ... (5.25). From the equation of continuity A1 v1 = A2 v2, v1 = A2 v2 / A1. As A2 is small compared with A1, v1 is small compared with v2: the fluid in the wider portion is very slow compared with the narrow portion, so v1 can be neglected on the right-hand side of Eq. 5.25: P1 - P2 = (1/2) rho v2^2 ... (5.26). This is the Venturi relation, used in the Venturi meter, a device to measure the speed of liquid flow. It is clear from Bernoulli's equation for a horizontal pipe that where the speed is high the pressure will be low: P + (1/2) rho v^2 = constant (Interesting Information).

A simple application of Bernoulli's equation: suppose a large tank of fluid has two small orifices A and B (Fig. 5.23). To find the speed with which water flows from orifice A: since the orifices are so small, the efflux speeds v2 and v3 are much larger than the speed v1 of the top surface of the water, so v1 can be taken as approximately zero. Bernoulli's equation then reads P1 + rho g h1 = P2 + (1/2) rho v2^2 + rho g h2; but P1 = P2 = atmospheric pressure, so v2 = sqrt(2 g (h1 - h2)) ... (5.27). This is Torricelli's theorem: the speed of efflux is equal to the velocity gained by the fluid in falling through the distance (h1 - h2) under the action of gravity. The speed of efflux is the same as that of a ball falling through the height (h1 - h2): the top level of the tank has moved down a little and the PE has been transferred into the KE of the efflux. If the orifice had been pointed upward at B (the print cites 'Fig. 6.4', which does not exist in this chapter), this KE would allow the liquid to rise to the level of the water in the tank; in practice viscous-energy losses alter the result to some extent.

blocks.prompt: A tank has a hole 5 m below the water surface; find the efflux speed (numerical 5.7). Why is it dangerous to stand near a fast-moving train, and how does a venturi mask work (short question 5.9; MCQ 5.11)?
blocks.explanation: v = sqrt(2 g h) = sqrt(2 x 9.8 x 5) = 9.9 m s^-1. The air dragged along by the train moves fast, so its pressure is lower than the still air behind you, and the pressure difference pushes you towards the train. In a venturi mask oxygen passing a narrow jet moves fast and lowers the pressure, drawing in a fixed proportion of room air: Bernoulli's principle.

items: Fast fluid, low pressure: wing lift (streamlines closer above), swing of a spinning ball (Magnus effect), filter pump, carburetor (Venturi duct), paint sprayer and atomizer.
Venturi: horizontal pipe, P1 - P2 = (1/2) rho (v2^2 - v1^2), with v1 negligible P1 - P2 = (1/2) rho v2^2 (Venturi meter). Torricelli: v2 = sqrt(2 g (h1 - h2)), the free-fall speed through the depth.
